papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Deer keds are blood-feeding ectoparasites of cervids and can carry diverse microorganisms of veterinary or potential zoonotic relevance. Nationwide information on their distribution, mitochondrial diversity, and associated microorganisms has been lacking in the Republic of Korea (ROK). This study investigated deer keds collected from cervids across the ROK and characterized their species identity, COX1 diversity, and sequence-confirmed microorganisms. A total of 405 deer keds were opportunistically collected from 116 cervids made available through ongoing regional wildlife management activities across nine provinces of the Republic of Korea, including Korean water deer (Hydropotes inermis) on the mainland and Siberian roe deer (Capreolus pygargus) on Jeju Island. All 405 specimens were examined morphologically, and 186 were analyzed using cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COX1) sequencing for molecular confirmation and population-genetic analysis. Selected viral, bacterial, and protozoan microorganisms were screened using pooled qPCR/qRT-PCR or conventional PCR, followed by individual conventional PCR and Sanger sequencing for confirmation. Host-level clustering was evaluated using binomial generalized linear mixed models when sufficient confirmed detections were available. All 405 deer keds were identified morphologically as Lipoptena fortisetosa, and all 186 COX1-sequenced specimens were molecularly consistent with this identification. The 617-bp COX1 dataset comprised 29 haplotypes (Hd = 0.681 ± 0.038; π = 0.01262 ± 0.00101). AMOVA showed significant mitochondrial differentiation between Jeju Island and mainland samples (ΦST = 0.615, P < 0.001), although host species and geography were completely confounded. Sequence-confirmed microorganisms included Bartonella spp. in 94/405 deer keds (23.21%), Theileria spp. in 40/405 (9.88%), Coxiella-like organisms in 4/405 (0.99%), and Anaplasma capra in 2/405 (0.49%). No sequence-confirmed Babesia spp., Ehrlichia spp., Borrelia spp., Hepatozoon spp., or SFTSV were obtained. Bartonella detection showed very strong host-level clustering and a marked Jeju-mainland contrast, whereas Theileria detection did not differ significantly between regions after accounting for host clustering. Lipoptena fortisetosa was widely associated with the cervids examined across the ROK and showed substantial mitochondrial genetic structure between the sampled Jeju and mainland groups. Bartonella spp. were the most frequently sequence-confirmed microorganisms, followed by Theileria spp. Molecular detection alone does not establish vector competence, and the geographic and host-species effects in the present sampling design cannot be separated. Standardized longitudinal sampling and host-vector-microorganism interaction studies are required to clarify transmission ecology and population structure.

papers.title: IL36γ signaling promotes mammalian anti-tick immunity.
papers.abstract: Ticks, like Ixodes scapularis, can parasitize a diverse array of vertebrates, favoring natural hosts but feeding opportunistically on others. Natural hosts, as well as permissive hosts such as laboratory mice, tolerate repeated infestations, while many incidental hosts may acquire anti-tick immunity, as first described in guinea pigs. We show that tick-immune guinea pigs display altered dermal cytology and a distinct transcriptome, predominantly upregulating the IL36γ cytokine. Interference with IL36γ signaling, via gene knockdown, chemical inhibition, or its natural antagonist IL36RN, reversed anti-tick immunity in guinea pigs. Conversely, genome engineering to silence IL36RN in C3H mice, representing a permissive host, disrupted tick engorgement, interfering with the transmission of Lyme disease pathogens. These findings firmly establish IL36γ as a central mediator of protective anti-tick immunity involving I. scapularis in mammalian hosts and support future strategies to interfere with tick-transmitted infections.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The white-footed mouse, Peromyscus leucopus, is a generalist species found throughout the eastern and central United States that serves as an important reservoir for many tick-borne pathogens relevant to human health. Patterns of P. leucopus relative abundance within small mammal communities have been shown to correlate with the prevalence of Borrelia burgdorferi, the main causative agent of Lyme disease, in vector species. However, efforts to investigate patterns of P. leucopus population size and small mammal community structure often lack geographic variation. In this study, we characterized patterns of P. leucopus population size and small mammal community species richness across a broad geographic range in Pennsylvania. Population sizes and small mammal community richness values in northeastern Pennsylvania (mean   N ^     = 28.6; mean richness = 5.3) were greater than those in northwestern Pennsylvania (mean   N ^     = 19.7; mean richness = 2.8). Projected changes in climate and the expansion of human-caused disturbance have the potential to greatly influence the prevalence of P. leucopus in small mammal communities, so regular characterizations of P. leucopus community dynamics will likely be helpful to inform projections and assessments of human exposure to tick-borne pathogen risk.

papers.title: Type I interferon signaling promotes early innate control of Borrelia burgdorferi infection.
papers.abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, elicits a robust type I interferon (IFN-I) response that has been strongly associated with chronic inflammatory manifestations such as Lyme arthritis. Although IFN-I is known to be induced early during infection, its functional role in the initial stages of B. burgdorferi infection remains unclear. Here, we identify a protective role for IFN-I signaling in the early control of B. burgdorferi. At 5 days post-challenge, mice lacking the type I interferon receptor (IFNAR1) exhibited markedly elevated spirochetal burdens at the site of inoculation, indicating that IFN-I signaling contributes to restricting early bacterial expansion. By 10 days post-challenge, IFNAR1 deficiency resulted in significantly increased bacterial loads in the skin and a trend toward higher loads in heart tissues, while joint burdens remained unaffected. Mechanistically, IFN-I signaling enhanced macrophage uptake of B. burgdorferi, phagosomal processing, and intracellular killing, while also modulating inflammatory cytokine responses and promoting macrophage recruitment to the inoculation site. Conversely, pharmacological activation of IFN-I signaling augmented macrophage antimicrobial function and improved bacterial clearance. Together, these findings establish IFN-I as a key component of early host defense against B. burgdorferi and reveal a time-dependent role for IFN-I signaling in Lyme disease pathogenesis, with protective functions during early infection that contrast with its pathogenic effects at later stages.

papers.title: Molecular Screening of Arthropod-Borne Pathogens in Domestic Cats from Northeast of Mexico: First Report of Infection and Coinfection in the Country.
papers.abstract: Cat-associated pathogens transmitted by arthropods are of global public and veterinary health importance. Cats, as well as dogs, have historically coexisted with humans in rural and urban environments. However, studies on microorganisms associated with cats are much less extensive than those on dogs. Therefore, the present study aims to document natural infections of Anaplasma, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, and Rickettsia in cats (Felis catus) using PCR in northeastern Mexico. Blood samples were collected from cats with the support of the Canine and Feline Control Centers and veterinary clinics. Specific pathogens were amplified by PCR, and some positive samples were sequenced. A total of 250 cats were obtained from three municipalities in Nuevo Leon, Mexico. Specific PCR testing showed that 33.6% (84/250) cats tested positive for at least one of the pathogens. The overall natural pathogen infection rates were Ehrlichia with 20.8% (52/250), followed by Anaplasma with 8% (20/250), Bartonella with 3.2% (8/250), and Rickettsia with 1.6% (4/250). Phylogenetic analysis placed the Bartonella sequence within a well-supported B. quintana clade. The partial 16S rRNA sequence obtained from Ehrlichia was conservatively classified as Ehrlichia sp. closely related to E. chaffeensis. These findings document exposure or infection of cats with multiple arthropod-borne bacteria and support continued molecular surveillance using additional discriminatory loci.

papers.title: Circulating IP-10/CXCL10 Correlates With Parasitemia and Disease Severity in Patients With Babesiosis: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Human babesiosis is an emerging tick-borne zoonosis that can cause serious complications, including death. Immune mechanisms that confer protection or promote disease severity in human babesiosis are poorly understood. We measured the cytokine and antibody profile in a cohort of hospitalized patients who had babesiosis. Cytokine levels were measured in plasma using the Bio-Plex Pro Human Cytokine 27-Plex Assay, and Babesia microti-specific total IgG and its 4 isotypes were measured using an immunofluorescence assay. Cytokine profile was analyzed in relation to immune status, peak parasitemia, lowest hemoglobin levels, and disease severity. There were enhanced levels of 8 cytokines (eotaxin, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IP-10/CXCL10, MCP-1, MIP-1α, and TNF-α) in the plasma of 16 patients with babesiosis as compared with 7 controls. A positive correlation was found between IP-10 levels and parasitemia (Spearman R = 0.52, P = .04). Patients with severe babesiosis had elevated levels of IP-10 and IL-5 as compared with the other 2 clinical categories (ie, moderate and moderately severe). Immunosuppression was associated with low levels of the VEGF and FGF basic angiogenic factors. There was also an inverse correlation between hemoglobin and IL-1β or IL-9 levels. Last, patients with babesiosis produced abundant levels of immunofluorescence assay total IgG and IgG1 and IgG3 but low levels of IgG2 and no IgG4. IP-10 and other cytokines that exhibited elevated levels should be further investigated as biomarkers of severe babesiosis.

papers.title: Phylogenetic Profiling and Molecular Detection of Babesia and Theileria spp. in Ticks Infesting Livestock Across Kashmir Valley, India.
papers.abstract: Ticks are major vectors of protozoan hemoparasites, particularly Babesia and Theileria, causing substantial morbidity and economic losses in livestock. Data on molecular prevalence and circulating species in the high-altitude Kashmir Valley are limited. This study investigated the prevalence, distribution, and phylogenetic relationships of piroplasm infections in ticks infesting domestic ruminants. A cross-sectional survey was conducted across eight districts of the Kashmir Valley. A total of 4,965 livestock animals were examined, of which 1,800 were found tick-infested, yielding an overall infestation rate of 36.27%. Collected ticks were morphologically identified and screened for Babesia and Theileria DNA using genus-specific 18 S rRNA PCR. Positive amplicons were sequenced and subjected to phylogenetic analysis. Of the 1,800 ticks examined, Haemaphysalis constituted 1,529 (84.0%), followed by Rhipicephalus 171 (9.5%) and Ornithodoros 100 (5.5%). Overall PCR positivity was 19/1,800 (1.06%) for Babesia spp. and 10/1,800 (0.56%) for Theileria spp. Babesia DNA was detected in ticks from cattle (3/720; 0.42%), sheep (14/720; 1.94%), and goats (2/360; 0.56%), whereas Theileria DNA was detected in ticks from cattle (5/720; 0.69%) and goats (5/360; 1.39%). Female ticks showed significantly higher Babesia positivity than males (13/648; 2.01% vs. 3/792; 0.38%; P = 0.004). Tick infestation peaked during summer months. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the Kashmir Babesia sequences clustered with B. bovis reference sequences, while the Theileria sequences clustered with T. cf. luwenshuni-related sequences. This molecular and phylogenetic study provides evidence of B. bovis and T. luwenshuni-like sequences in ticks collected from livestock in the Kashmir Valley. Haemaphysalis was the predominant tick genus associated with the detected piroplasmid infections. Although overall PCR positivity was low, the findings provide baseline data for piroplasm surveillance and support further characterization using higher-resolution molecular markers.

papers.title: Molecular detection of pathogens in Rhipicephalus ticks collected from companion animals in Bejaia province, northern Algeria.
papers.abstract: Ticks are increasingly recognized as important vectors of pathogens affecting animals and humans worldwide. In northern Algeria, data on tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) in ixodid ticks collected from companion animals are still scarce. This pilot study is the first molecular investigation of TBPs in ixodid ticks collected from companion animals in Bejaia province, bordering the Mediterranean Sea. A total of 100 ticks were collected from 75 dogs, 11 cats, and one tortoise. Rhipicephalus sanguineus was the predominant tick species identified (99/100; 99%; 95% CI: 94.0-100.0), whereas a single tick collected from the tortoise was identified as Hyalomma aegyptium (1/100; 1%; 95% CI: 0-6.0). Ticks were tested for Rickettsia spp., Bartonella spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia canis, Piroplasmida, and Hepatozoon spp. Only Rickettsia spp. (11/100; 11%; 95% CI: 6.1-18.8), Hepatozoon spp. (6/100; 6%; 95% CI: 2.5-12.7) and Piroplasmida (2/100; 2%; 95% CI: 0.1-7.4) were detected. Rickettsia spp. (11/88; 12.5%; 95% CI: 7.0-21.2) and Piroplasmida (2/88; 2.3%; 95% CI: 0.1-8.4) were found only in ticks from dogs, while Hepatozoon spp. was found in both ticks from dogs (3/88; 3.4%; 95% CI: 0.8-9.7) and cats (3/11; 27.3%; 95% CI: 9.2-57.1). Further molecular characterization revealed R. massiliae and R. conorii, as well as H. canis, Babesia vogeli, and Cytauxzoon spp. Phylogenetic analysis supported species identification. These findings highlight the presence of TBPs in ticks from companion animals and their potential relevance to One Health, particularly for zoonotic Rickettsia spp.

papers.title: A Case Report of Lyme Carditis Presenting as New-Onset Atrial Flutter in the Emergency Department.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease (LD) is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States and has several well-known pathologic sequelae if not treated, including third-degree atrioventricular block. However, an association between Lyme carditis and atrial arrhythmias has been described in some cardiology literature but has not been reported in emergency medicine or wilderness medicine literature. This case report describes an older adult with new-onset atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rate in the setting of early disseminated LD, who ultimately was treated with antibiotics, had resolution of atrial flutter, and has had no recurrence. As cardiac inflammation secondary to organ infection may manifest as multiple forms of arrhythmia, this case report highlights the importance of considering LD as a differential diagnosis when treating tick-exposed patients with new cardiac arrhythmias, including atrial flutter.

papers.title: Borrelia garinii spirochetemia in a previously healthy child presenting with Streptococcus anginosus group brain abscess: a case report.
papers.abstract: The clinical significance of transient Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex (hereafter referred to as B. burgdorferi) spirochetemia remains poorly understood and has rarely been documented. We report the isolation of viable B. garinii genospecies from the blood of a previously healthy child presenting with a Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) brain abscess. An eight-year-old girl presented with four days of headache, fever, nausea, slightly reduced general condition, and mild facial asymmetry. Initial evaluation, including lumbar puncture, raised suspicion of viral meningitis or Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB). Based on the differential diagnosis of Lyme disease, she was enrolled in the prospective BRILLIANT study (NCT06045416), with additional blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling for B. burgdorferi culture and serology. Following initial outpatient management, she re-presented with clinical deterioration and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed a brain abscess requiring surgical drainage. Abscess cultures yielded SAG. Dental treatment four days before symptom onset provided a plausible source of infectious spread. Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for six weeks resulted in complete clinical recovery and radiological improvement. Borrelia burgdorferi-specific two-tier serology and CSF culture remained negative. In contrast, blood plasma culture for B. burgdorferi obtained at initial presentation yielded viable spirochetes after seven weeks. Borrelia burgdorferi DNA was confirmed by flaB-targeted qPCR, and hybrid whole-genome sequencing generated a near-complete genome identifying B. garinii genospecies. This case demonstrates viable B. garinii spirochetemia without serological evidence of LNB, incidentally detected during investigation of a SAG brain abscess. It highlights the uncertain clinical significance of transient B. burgdorferi spirochetemia, and the importance of interpreting microbiological findings within the clinical context.

papers.title: Lyme Disease and Other Tick-Borne Infections.
papers.abstract: The neurologic manifestations of selected tick-transmitted infections in North America and Eurasia were reviewed. Both Powassan virus in North America, and Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE) virus in Eurasia can cause encephalitis, often with significant neurologic morbidity. Lyme disease, Ehrlichia chaffeensis (the cause of human monocytic ehrlichiosis [HME]), and Borrelia miyamotoi infections can cause meningitis (the third primarily in immunocompromised individuals). Patients with Lyme disease may also develop cranial neuropathy, and/or radiculoneuropathy. Tick-borne infections are being increasingly recognized in North America and Eurasia. While many tick-borne infections can cause headaches, lethargy or other non-specific symptoms, these are generally not evidence of nervous system infection - i.e., neuroinvasive disease. The latter is less common but may occur in infections due to Powassan and TBE viruses, in HME and in Lyme disease. Patients with symptomatic nervous system infection due to Powassan or TBE virus are at high risk of developing significant neurologic impairment and sequelae.

papers.title: Anaplasma spp., Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria Infections in Vermipsylla Alakurt Fleas.
papers.abstract: Vermipsylla alakurt (Siphonaptera: Vermipsyllidae) is mainly distributed in alpine areas of north-western China, infesting sheep, goat and yaks, causing pruritus, anaemia and losses to animal husbandry. The carriage of vector-borne pathogens by this flea remains unclear. In January 2025, 89 fleas were collected from sheep in the China-Kazakhstan border area of northwest China and identified as V. alakurt by morphology and COII gene sequencing. Multiple genetic markers targeting the genera of Anaplasma, Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria were amplified and sequenced. Among 83 female fleas, Anaplasma ovis (n = 6), Coxiella burnetii (n = 37), Babesia sp. (n = 7), Babesia ovis (n = 1) and Theileria annulata (n = 4) were identified. The co-infection of Coxiella burnetii with Anaplasma ovis and Theileria annulata were respectively found. Multiple typical vector-borne pathogens were detected at the first time in V. alakurt fleas. This finding indicates that V. alakurt fleas can carry Anaplasma, Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria in the alpine region of the China-Kazakhstan border.

papers.title: Functional Metagenomics Reveals Gut Microbial Biosynthetic Potential for Essential Nutrients in Juvenile Chum Salmon.
papers.abstract: The fish gut microbiota contributes to host nutrition, immunity and homeostasis, yet how its metabolic capacity relates to gaps in the host genome remains poorly characterized. Here we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing and KEGG module completion analysis to compare the biosynthetic potential of the gut microbiome with that of the host genome in juvenile chum salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) at 35 days posthatching, when exogenous feeding begins. Because small juvenile guts yield low microbial biomass and a high proportion of host DNA, we first optimized a protocol combining enzymatic lysis with NEBNext-based host DNA depletion. This raised the bacterial sequence fraction from 11.3% to 41.2% and increased the number of KEGG Orthology identifiers mapped to modules from 1128 to 1532. Module Completion Ratio analysis revealed complementation in functional potential: the chum salmon genome was incomplete for de novo biosynthesis of essential amino acids (threonine, leucine, valine/isoleucine, lysine) and B-vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin, biotin), whereas the gut metagenome encoded complete or near-complete modules for these pathways. Sequences assigned to Bartonella-like, Acinetobacter and Enterococcus lineages contributed most. These observations indicate that the gut microbiome encodes biosynthetic potential the host genome lacks, although demonstrating a nutritional benefit to the host will require experimental manipulation.

papers.title: Development and validation of a recombinant chimeric antigen based on Leishmania infantum B-cell epitopes for canine serology.
papers.abstract: This study describes the development and validation of a novel multi-epitope chimeric protein (rChi) for the serodiagnosis of canine leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum (CanL). The rChi construct was engineered based on B-cell epitopes from hypothetical proteins previously identified through immunoproteomic profiling. To evaluate its diagnostic performance, an indirect ELISA was conducted using a comprehensive panel of canine serum samples (n = 291), including clinically affected, subclinically infected, and non-infected dogs, as well as Leish-Tec®-vaccinated animals and those infected with potentially cross-reactive pathogens (Babesia vogeli, Ehrlichia canis, and Trypanosoma cruzi). The rChi-ELISA demonstrated superior diagnostic parameters compared to L. infantum soluble Leishmania antigen (SLA), achieving 92.2% sensitivity and 76.2% specificity (AUC = 0.85; Accuracy = 80.8%), whereas SLA showed only 50.0% sensitivity and 68.3% accuracy. These findings indicate that the rChi protein significantly enhances CanL detection and represents a promising tool for more accurate veterinary diagnostics and surveillance.

papers.title: Molecular evidence of Bartonella spp. in wild felids from Brazil.
papers.abstract: Among Felidae, domestic cats play a role as reservoirs for Bartonella henselae, Bartonella clarridgeiae, and Bartonella koehlerae. Despite the well-known relationship between Bartonella spp. and domestic cats, to date, there is still a paucity of reports on Bartonella spp. in wild felids. The aim of this study was to molecularly detect and characterize Bartonella spp. in blood and tissue samples from wild felids sampled in Brazil. Among 291 DNA samples (211 blood, 77 spleens and three livers), 3.09% (9/291) were positive in the Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qPCR) assay for Bartonella spp. based on the nuoG gene: 1/44 Leopardus pardalis, 3/61 Leopardus geoffroyi, 1/66 Panthera onca, 1/3 Herpailurus yagouaroundi, and 3/32 Leopardus wiedii. In the phylogenetic analyses, while the gltA sequence detected in L. wiedii grouped with Bartonella henselae, the gltA and ftsZ sequences detected in L. geoffroyi clustered within the same subclade as Bartonella sp. sequences previously identified in wild rodents and associated fleas. These findings reinforce that besides harboring Bartonella species associated with cats, wild felids also may act as accidental hosts for Bartonella species associated with wild small mammals, possibly as a consequence of predation.

papers.title: [Bed bugs, lice and fleas-an up-to-date overview of diagnosis, treatment and prevention].
papers.abstract: Despite high standards of hygiene, ectoparasites remain a significant issue in dermatology. Bedbugs (Cimex lectularius) have become significantly more prevalent worldwide over the past two decades, whilst head lice infestation (Pediculus humanus capitis) remains one of the most common parasitic infections in children. Pubic lice (Pthirus pubis) are predominantly transmitted sexually. Body lice (Pediculus humanus corporis) are rare in Central Europe, but remain of infectious disease significance as vectors of Rickettsia prowazekii, Bartonella quintana and Borrelia recurrentis. Flea bites in humans are now predominantly caused by the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis). The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic cases through papular and urticarial reactions to bullous arthropod reactions and bacterial superinfections. Diagnosis is based on medical history, clinical findings and the direct detection of parasites, nits or characteristic environmental traces. Dermoscopy facilitates the differentiation of live parasites from nits and pseudonits, particularly in cases of pediculosis. Treatment for lice infestations comprises topical pediculicides and physically acting preparations. In the case of bedbug and flea infestations, consistent environmental control measures are crucial for long-term therapeutic success; in the case of flea infestations, concurrent veterinary treatment of infested pets is also essential. This article summarises the current state of knowledge regarding the epidemiology, biology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of these medically important ectoparasitic infestations. Ektoparasiten stellen trotz hoher Hygienestandards weiterhin ein relevantes Thema in der Dermatologie dar. Bettwanzenbefälle (Cimex lectularius) haben in den vergangenen 2 Jahrzehnten weltweit deutlich zugenommen, während der Kopflausbefall (Pediculus humanus capitis) unverändert zu den häufigsten parasitären Erkrankungen im Kindesalter zählt. Filzläuse (Pthirus pubis) werden überwiegend sexuell übertragen. Kleiderläuse (Pediculus humanus corporis) sind in Mitteleuropa selten, besitzen jedoch als Vektoren von Rickettsia prowazekii, Bartonella quintana und Borrelia recurrentis weiterhin infektiologische Bedeutung. Flohstiche beim Menschen werden heute überwiegend durch den Katzenfloh (Ctenocephalides felis) verursacht. Das klinische Spektrum reicht von asymptomatischen Verläufen über papulöse und urtikarielle Reaktionen bis hin zu bullösen Arthropodenreaktionen und bakteriellen Superinfektionen. Die Diagnostik basiert auf Anamnese, klinischem Befund sowie dem direkten Nachweis von Parasiten, Nissen oder charakteristischen Umweltspuren. Die Dermatoskopie erleichtert insbesondere bei Pedikulosen die Differenzierung vitaler Parasiten von Nissen und Pseudonissen. Die Therapie umfasst bei Läuseinfestationen topische Pedikulozide und physikalisch wirkende Präparate. Bei Bettwanzen- und Flohbefall sind konsequente Umgebungsmaßnahmen sowie beim Flohbefall die veterinärmedizinische Mitbehandlung befallener Haustiere entscheidend für den nachhaltigen Therapieerfolg. Der Beitrag fasst den aktuellen Kenntnisstand zu Epidemiologie, Biologie, Klinik, Diagnostik, Therapie und Prävention dieser wichtigen humanmedizinisch relevanten Ektoparasitosen zusammen.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The family Borreliaceae comprises the genera Cristispira and Borrelia, the latter including the subgenera Borrelia and Borreliella. Australia hosts a unique assemblage of wildlife and tick species that may support the circulation of indigenous Borrelia lineages. A narrative review of the available literature was conducted to summarize current knowledge of the taxonomy, diversity, ecology, tick associations, vertebrate hosts, and potential public health significance of Borreliaceae detected in Australia. The diversity of Australian Borrelia is currently represented by members of the relapsing fever (RF) and Echidna-Reptile (REP) groups. These include Borrelia queenslandica, Borrelia sp. HB, Candidatus Borrelia tachyglossi, Ca. B. undatumii, and Ca. B. rubricentralis, which have been detected in association with native wildlife and tick species. However, vector competence has not yet been demonstrated for most tick-associated Borrelia lineages identified in Australia. To date, no indigenous member of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex has been convincingly detected in Australian ticks, wildlife, or humans. Nevertheless, persistent symptom complexes following tick exposure have been reported and are currently grouped under the umbrella term Debilitating Symptom Complexes Attributed to Ticks (DSCATT). Current evidence indicates that Australian Borreliaceae fauna is dominated by indigenous relapsing fever and reptile-associated lineages rather than Lyme borreliosis agents. Further genomic, ecological, reservoir-host, and vector-competence studies are needed to clarify their transmission cycles, evolutionary relationships, zoonotic potential, and their significance within a One Health framework.

papers.title: Vector-borne zoonotic bacteria in Tunisia: from fragmented data to an integrated One Health surveillance framework.
papers.abstract: Vector-borne and vector-associated bacterial zoonoses represent an important component of infectious disease epidemiology in Tunisia. This review synthesizes available evidence on major bacterial groups, including Rickettsia, Bartonella, Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Borrelia, Coxiella burnetii, and other arthropod-associated bacteria, using a One Health framework integrating human, animal, vector, wildlife, and environmental compartments. The available evidence reveals heterogeneous levels of knowledge across bacterial taxa. Rickettsia represents the most established tick-associated zoonotic system, with Rickettsia conorii as the main confirmed human pathogen, while additional species have been detected mainly in arthropods or animal-associated settings. Bartonella has a significant clinical association with blood culture-negative endocarditis, whereas other bacterial groups show predominantly animal- or vector-associated evidence. Coxiella burnetii remains a major zoonotic concern linked to livestock, camels, reproductive materials, and environmental exposure. For Borrelia, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia, substantial evidence of circulation exists in vectors and animals, but human clinical relevance remains incompletely characterized. Across bacterial groups, a recurrent limitation is the imbalance between molecular detection in vectors or animal hosts and confirmed evidence of transmission or human disease. Detection of bacterial DNA should therefore be interpreted cautiously and not considered equivalent to infection, reservoir competence, or vectorial transmission. Additional arthropod-associated bacteria identified through microbiome studies require further investigation to clarify their ecological significance. The Tunisian evidence base demonstrates active circulation of diverse vector-associated bacteria but remains fragmented across clinical, veterinary, entomological, and ecological domains. Strengthening integrated One Health surveillance through coordinated human diagnosis, animal sentinel systems, vector monitoring, environmental investigations, and advanced molecular approaches is essential to better assess zoonotic risks in Tunisia and the wider North African-Mediterranean region.

papers.title: Disseminated Bartonella washoensis infection in a kidney transplant recipient diagnosed by 16S rRNA next-generation sequencing: A case report.
papers.abstract: Bartonella species are increasingly recognized as causes of invasive infections in immunocompromised hosts. We report the first case in Colombia of disseminated Bartonella washoensis infection in a kidney transplant recipient. A 43-year-old woman receiving maintenance immunosuppression presented with prolonged fever, constitutional symptoms, abdominal pain, multiple splenic lesions, and vertebral osteomyelitis. Extensive microbiological, serological, and molecular investigations were initially negative. Due to persistent fever and diagnostic uncertainty, a diagnostic splenectomy was performed, which revealed necrotizing granulomas. Broad-range bacterial 16S rRNA next-generation sequencing of splenic tissue identified B. washoensis, establishing the diagnosis of disseminated bartonellosis. Targeted antimicrobial therapy resulted in clinical and radiological improvement without recurrence during follow-up. This case highlights the potential for rare zoonotic Bartonella species to cause disseminated disease in transplant recipients and underscores the diagnostic value of broad-range bacterial 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing when conventional diagnostic methods are unrevealing.

papers.title: [What should you request to the laboratory for a patient bitten by a tick ?].
papers.abstract: Ticks are a growing concern for the public, owing to their abundance and a longer activity season. In Switzerland, more than 99% of ticks removed from humans are of the species Ixodes ricinus. This article reviews the tick-borne diseases documented in the country : Lyme borreliosis, tick-borne encephalitis, tularaemia, neoehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, Borrelia miyamotoi relapsing fever, and rickettsiosis. Carriage of a microorganism by a tick does not imply infection, just as isolated seropositivity does not imply disease. Testing should be guided by pretest probability and disease stage, using validated assays only. Here, the laboratory is a key partner : it guides test selection and the interpretation of results, helping to avoid both under and overdiagnosis. Les tiques inquiètent la population, du fait de leur abondance et d’une saison d’activité prolongée. En Suisse, plus de 99 % des tiques retirées de l’homme sont de l’espèce Ixodes ricinus. Cet article passe en revue les maladies vectorielles à tiques documentées dans le pays : borréliose de Lyme, méningo-encéphalite verno-estivale, tularémie, neoehrlichiose, anaplasmose, babésiose, fièvre récurrente à Borrelia miyamotoi et rickettsioses. Le portage d’un micro-organisme par la tique ne signifie pas une infection, comme une séropositivité isolée ne signifie pas une maladie. Le choix des examens doit reposer sur la probabilité prétest et le stade clinique, en privilégiant les tests validés. Le laboratoire est ici un partenaire essentiel : il oriente leur prescription et l’interprétation des résultats, évitant aussi bien le sous-diagnostic que le surdiagnostic.

papers.title: Honey Bees as Bioindicators of Environmental PFASs Contamination and Potential Effects on Gut-Microbial Communities.
papers.abstract: Honey bees are valuable bioindicators of environmental contamination due to their wide foraging range and exposure to diverse biotic and abiotic stressors. This study evaluates the use of honey bees as bioindicators for detecting per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in areas with varying levels of exposure risk (high-, intermediate-, and low-), as well as their potential effects on gut-microbial communities. Analytical chemistry to detect PFASs and pesticide residues were combined with molecular and metagenomic analyses to identify common honey bee pathogens and characterize gut-microbial communities. Short-chain PFASs were predominated over long-chain compounds, particularly in high-risk areas, while pesticide residues occurred in only a few apiaries. Molecular analyses revealed several widespread pathogens, while metagenomics showed a stable gut microbiome mainly composed of the genera Lactobacillus, Bartonella, Bombilactobacillus, Snodgrassella, Gilliamella, Bifidobacterium, and Gluconacetobacter. However, microbial-community composition differed significantly between apiaries with high- versus low-risk PFAS exposure. These results support honey bees as effective bioindicators for environmental PFAS monitoring and suggest that PFAS exposure may be associated with alterations in their gut-microbial communities. Further research is needed to elucidate the impact of PFASs on honey bee toxicity, gut-microbiota composition, and overall health.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), caused by Borrelia garinii, often leads to persistent neurological deficits, yet early diagnosis remains insensitive and the temporal metabolic changes in the infected brain are largely unexplored. In this study, a murine model of B. garinii infection was established using 80 female BALB/c mice, and brain tissues were collected at acute 7 (days post-infection, DPI), mid- (15 and 21 DPI), and chronic (30 DPI) stages for untargeted gas chromatography-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOF-MS) metabolomics. Thirty-one differential metabolites were identified, with downregulated metabolites predominating acutely and upregulated metabolites prevailing chronically. Twelve common metabolites, including creatine, lysine, and galactose derivatives, were consistently altered. KEGG analysis revealed disrupted amino acid metabolism, particularly valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis (ko00290), arginine and proline metabolism (ko00330), and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis (ko00970). ROC analysis identified five candidate biomarkers, hydroxylamine, 2,3-dihydroxypyridine, galactose 1, galactose 2, and monostearin, with high diagnostic accuracy. This study provides a comprehensive temporal metabolomic landscape of the brain during B. garinii infection, revealing time-dependent metabolic reprogramming with sustained disruptions in amino acid and energy metabolism, and offering candidate biomarkers for improved diagnosis of central nervous system involvement in Lyme disease.

papers.title: Retrospective Serological Survey of Equine Influenza Virus and Piroplasm Parasites in Free-Ranging Wild Equids from Kenya and Tanzania.
papers.abstract: Wild equids may act as reservoirs for infectious pathogens affecting domestic equine populations, yet data on exposure to equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV), equine influenza virus (EIV), and equine piroplasmosis agents in African wildlife remain scarce. Our objectives were to retrospectively determine serological evidence of exposure to EIAV, EIV, Theileria equi, and Babesia caballi among Grevy's zebras and rhinoceroses from Kenya and Tanzania. A total of 284 archived serum samples from 215 Grevy's zebras and 69 rhinoceroses were analyzed using commercial ELISAs. Positive EIAV screening tests were retested using a second confirmatory assay. No confirmed EIAV antibodies were detected in zebras or rhinoceroses. Antibodies against EIV were identified in 20/215 zebras (9.3%), all originating from Serengeti National Park. Theileria equi antibodies were detected in 194/206 zebras (94.2%), while Babesia caballi antibodies were detected in 8/206 zebras (3.9%). Rhinoceroses were negative for all pathogens tested. This study provides evidence of widespread exposure of Grevy's zebras to T. equi and limited exposure to EIV in East Africa while failing to identify serologic evidence of EIAV infection in zebras or rhinoceroses. These findings improve understanding of infectious disease ecology at the wildlife-livestock interface and support continued wildlife surveillance programs.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Theileria annulata causes tropical theileriosis in cattle and is endemic in Kazakhstan. Although molecular diagnostic methods for this pathogen exist, data on its molecular surveillance and genetic diversity in Kazakhstan remain limited. This study aimed to develop and experimentally validate a species-specific real-time PCR (qPCR) assay for the detection of Theileria annulata and to conduct molecular surveillance and phylogenetic analysis of circulating isolates. A total of 709 cattle blood samples from 10 regions of Kazakhstan were analysed. Species-specific primers and a probe were designed targeting the 18S rRNA gene, and diagnostic performance was evaluated against sequencing as the reference method. Theileria annulata infection was confirmed in 110 of 709 samples (15.51%), with positive samples identified in the Turkistan, West Kazakhstan, Kyzylorda, and Zhambyl regions. The developed assay showed high diagnostic sensitivity (99.09%), specificity (99.67%), and diagnostic efficiency (99.58%), with no cross-reactivity with Theileria orientalis, Theileria parva, Babesia bovis, Babesia bigemina, or Anaplasma marginale. Phylogenetic analysis of partial 28S rRNA sequences confirmed the species identity of the detected isolates and demonstrated their close relationship with previously reported Kazakhstani and Chinese isolates. The developed qPCR assay is suitable for the molecular diagnosis and surveillance of bovine tropical theileriosis in Kazakhstan.

papers.title: Giving a Rat's: Acquisition of Baseline Health Data on Native Australian Rodents During a Conservation Translocation.
papers.abstract: Little is known about the baseline health status of Australia's native rodents. The resultant knowledge gaps are problematic for wildlife translocations, as assessing disease risk is integral to translocation planning and outcomes. A disease risk analysis was conducted for the conservation translocation of native rodents to Dirk Hartog Island, Western Australia. This analysis resulted in a recommendation for a multidisciplinary project to reduce knowledge gaps about the health status of Shark Bay mice (Pseudomys gouldii) and greater-stick-nest rats (Leporillus conditor). Between 2021 and 2022, 130 Shark Bay mice and 122 greater stick-nest rats were translocated to Dirk Hartog Island. Mucosal swabs, whole blood, faeces, and ectoparasites were collected from a subset of these individuals. Molecular testing for four infectious agents was performed, parasite burdens and haematological parameters were examined, and relationships between these variables, health metrics and post-translocation short-term survival were assessed. Necropsies with routine histological assessment on translocation mortalities were performed where feasible. Several indicators of non-infectious factors contributing to morbidity or mortality were found, highlighting the need to iteratively evaluate translocation strategies. There was also an apparent absence of some host-specific parasites, suggesting that active approaches to parasite conservation during translocations should be considered. Molecular evidence of herpesviruses, a paramyxovirus, Bartonella sp., Trypanosoma sp. and Mycoplasma spp. were detected among the translocated animals. Although not associated with morbidity or short-term mortality in this study, the disease potential of these agents is still present. Overall, these results contribute important new data on health baselines for both species, which will assist in informing future conservation planning.

papers.title: In situ structure of the flagellar export apparatus reveals membrane remodeling and lipid-mediated coupling between FlhA and the export gate.
papers.abstract: The transmembrane export apparatus is a conserved core of bacterial type III secretion systems shared by flagella and injectisomes. Powered by the proton-motive force (PMF), this machinery translocates protein substrates across the cytoplasmic membrane to support bacterial motility and virulence. However, how the export apparatus assembles and functions within native membranes remains poorly understood. Here, using in situ single-particle cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography, we resolve high-resolution structures of the flagellar export apparatus within intact cells of the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Structural and genetic analyses suggest that coordinated assembly of the export apparatus and MS-ring drives extensive deformation of the cytoplasmic membrane, generating a funnel-shaped conduit for substrate translocation. The FlhA nonamer and FliPQR-FlhB export gate lack direct transmembrane contacts and are separated by a thin, bilayer-like density, revealing a lipid-mediated interface. The conserved FlhB hinge helix extends into the FlhA tunnel and may couple PMF-driven energy transduction to substrate translocation. We further identify a conserved hydrophilic pathway within FlhA and show that key acidic residues lining this pathway are essential for export activity. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for export apparatus assembly and energy transduction, providing broader insights into type III secretion.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic parasite transmitted by ticks or through blood transfusion, and it can cause babesiosis with symptoms such as fever, anemia, and organ failure. The parasite is closely related to the mosquito-borne Plasmodium falciparum, which causes malaria. Several studies have shown that individuals with blood group O have a reduced risk of severe malaria compared to individuals with other ABO blood groups. Whether or not this is also the case for babesiosis has not yet been clearly investigated. In this study, serum samples from over 650 individuals were analyzed using an ELISA assay to detect antibodies against Babesia divergens. The ABO blood groups of the same samples were determined using a conventional method. There was no difference in B. divergens IgG antibody levels between the different ABO blood groups, nor was there any difference in the percentage of positive reactions in the ELISA against B. divergens between the different blood groups. This could indicate that the development and maintenance of B. divergens antibodies are not influenced by ABO blood groups.
